templates.name: Quiet Practice
templates.summary: A calm counselling site whose gentle four-question self-check routes visitors to the matching service page — individual, couples, or teen counselling — every page static and shareable.
templates.description:
Quiet Practice is a multi-page website for a solo therapist or counsellor whose real problem is not looking pretty online — it is that prospective clients arrive anxious, skim a wall of text, and leave without knowing which service was meant for them. Instead of a long about page, the site leads with a gentle "is this right for me?" check: four small questions, one at a time in large serif type, that end by landing the visitor on the service page that fits what they described. The result is a real, shareable URL — not a generic contact form — and the check is honestly framed as a signpost, not a clinical assessment, with a disclaimer and an email fallback for people nothing quite fits.

The seed content ships three services — individual therapy, couples counselling, and teen counselling — each with its own statically generated page: an "it might fit if" list, how sessions would work, what the first session is like, and a sticky session-details card with length, fee, rhythm, format, and the booking action. Routing is a small typed utility: every answer adds weighted points to one or more services, the highest total wins, and ties resolve to whichever service led earliest — so "who would the sessions be for?" carries the most signal but consistent later answers can override it. Every service page also appears in normal navigation (homepage index rows, footer, cross-links), loads directly at its own URL, and a noscript note points no-JavaScript visitors to the plain service list. The homepage rounds out with a three-step "how it starts" strip, a four-question FAQ with FAQPage JSON-LD, and a dusk-dark contact panel whose primary action is the configured booking link or a warm click-to-call fallback, with tel: and mailto: links always built from the same contact details shown on screen.

Everything a practice owner edits lives in three JSON files — site.json for names, credentials, phone, email, bookingUrl, hours, FAQs, and every section heading; services.json for the services, fees, and per-service accent tones; self-check.json for the questions and their routing weights — with scoring, contact-link, and currency-formatting logic kept in typed utilities. The design is a committed dusk-calm system: muted dusk blue, soft lavender, and warm grey on near-white paper, Source Serif 4 headings with IBM Plex Sans body, original abstract ripple SVG artwork instead of stock photography, and generous unhurried whitespace. Technically it is Nuxt 4 with Vue 3 and strict TypeScript, generated to fully static HTML (no server runtime) with all routes prerendered, ESLint flat config, vue-tsc type-checking in the build, reduced-motion support, visible focus states, semantic landmarks, and layouts verified down to 320 px wide.

The shipped demo demonstrates these capabilities directly. Standout details include Four-question self-check that routes to a service, Transparent weighted routing logic, Statically generated service pages, Honest booking handoff, and Homepage service index rows. Its content and state strategy uses committed JSON data and configuration. The stack uses Nuxt 4 (Vue 3), fully static via nuxt generate. Presentation uses plain hand-written CSS with centralized design tokens. This gives evaluators a working, customizable foundation rather than a static visual concept.

templates.name: Couch to 5K
templates.summary: A nine-week running plan visitors tick off session by session, with progress saved on their own phone.
templates.description:
Couch to 5K is a single-page training-plan site for a running coach whose beginner clients keep losing the printed handout. The classic nine-week walk-run progression — twenty-seven sessions of roughly half an hour — lives on one fast page the runner keeps open on their phone. Every session card carries a coach-style title, exact interval instructions such as "Run 1 min / walk 90 sec — repeat × 8", and an approximate duration, and every week comes with a short note in the coach's voice.

The page is built around progress the runner can feel. Ticking a session saves it to localStorage on the device — no account, no sync, nothing uploaded — and the ticks survive reloads and revisits. Per-week counters, segment bars, a sticky header with week chips 1–9, an aria-live "12 of 27 sessions done" counter, and a slim progress strip all update the moment a box is ticked, and an original SVG trail map in the hero fills in coral from START toward the 5K finish flag as weeks are completed in order. A reset control with an explicit confirm step clears the device, mailto and tel actions route enquiries straight to the coach, and a five-question FAQ ships with FAQPage JSON-LD. Because the site is fully prerendered, it even renders sensibly with JavaScript disabled — checkboxes still tick natively, they simply don't persist.

Personalization is two JSON files: src/lib/data/site.json holds the coach, contact, and FAQ copy, and src/lib/data/plan.json holds all nine weeks, so a coach can rewrite the whole programme without touching a component. The localStorage store, session-id scheme, and progress wording live in small typed modules, styling is hand-written CSS driven by coral/navy/off-white design tokens with the Sora typeface, and the build is SvelteKit 2 with Svelte 5 runes and adapter-static producing a fully static build/ directory that passes ESLint and svelte-check and stays overflow-free down to 320 px.

The shipped demo demonstrates these capabilities directly. Standout details include Tickable nine-week plan, On-device progress, Live progress indicators, SVG trail map, and Reset with confirm step. Its content and state strategy uses device-local localStorage state. The stack uses SvelteKit (Svelte 5) with @sveltejs/adapter-static — fully prerendered. Presentation uses hand-written CSS — design tokens in a global stylesheet plus scoped component styles. This gives evaluators a working, customizable foundation rather than a static visual concept.

templates.name: Movement Library
templates.summary: A physio exercise library where patients filter movements by body part, build a small home plan, and print it as a clean take-home card.
templates.description:
Movement Library is a single-page website for a physiotherapy or physical-therapy practice that wants every patient to leave with a clear, repeatable home plan. Between appointments patients forget doses, lose handout sheets, and give up hunting through video links; this template puts the clinic's ten most-prescribed movements on one page, each written exactly the way it is coached in the treatment room — body-part tags, sets and reps or hold times, two-to-three numbered steps, and an honest caution note. No video hosting, patient accounts, or booking system is required, and a visible note states plainly that the library is general guidance, not a personalised prescription.

The patient journey is deliberately small: filter, add, print. Anatomical-tag filter chips for Neck, Shoulder, Back, Hip, Knee, and Ankle carry live exercise counts and update a "Showing X of 10 movements" status line. Every movement is a chart-style card pairing an original line-figure illustration with a kinesiology-tape dosage strip, numbered coaching steps, and a highlighted "Take care" warning. Add-to-plan buttons fill a plan tray that docks to the bottom of the viewport once it holds movements, with per-item remove, clear, and print actions — and the plan persists in localStorage, so it survives reloads and return visits. The centerpiece is the print flow: a dedicated print stylesheet hides the entire app and outputs only a clean black-and-white patient card with the practice name and date, a write-in "Prepared for" line, each movement's figure, dose, steps, and caution, Mon–Sun adherence tick boxes, and the practice contact line with the guidance disclaimer.

Everything a practice needs to change lives in two committed JSON files: src/data/site.json holds the practice name, physiotherapist, phone, email, address, hero copy, disclaimer, tray and print-card labels, and five FAQs (rendered as an accessible accordion with FAQPage JSON-LD), while src/data/exercises.json holds the movements themselves — edit a dose or add an exercise and the filters, counts, tray, and printed card all follow. Call and email actions are real tel: and mailto: links built from the same displayed data. The design is an original warm clinic-chart direction — paper white, ink navy, and kinesiology-tape green with Zilla Slab and Figtree type, chart-paper grid textures, and ten hand-drawn SVG stick figures sharing one visual grammar. Built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite as a fully static SPA, it lints and type-checks clean, keeps controls keyboard-accessible with aria-pressed states, visible focus rings, and polite live regions, and stays free of horizontal overflow down to 320px-wide screens.

The shipped demo demonstrates these capabilities directly. Standout details include Body-part filter chips, Printable patient card, Persistent plan tray, plan tray, and dedicated print stylesheet. Its content and state strategy uses device-local localStorage state. The stack uses React and Vite. Presentation uses layered plain CSS with design tokens. This gives evaluators a working, customizable foundation rather than a static visual concept.

templates.description:
Client Gallery is the delivery page a wedding or event photographer sends when the final selection is ready. Handing over finished photographs is easy; getting a useful answer back is not — the edit conversation usually stalls on "which ones do you want printed, retouched, or in the album?". This template turns that question into the page itself: a private, single-page gallery where the couple simply stars what they love, and the reply writes itself.

The album opens on a print-room masthead — the couple's names in Libre Caslon serif, the event date, venue, photograph count, and a quiet "Photographed by" credit — then flows into a charcoal masonry wall of twelve matted frames, each with a proof-sheet number, a caption, and its exact filename. Every frame carries a real star button with aria-pressed state; favourites persist per device in localStorage keyed by the album id, so choosing can span several evenings. A sticky tray keeps the running count visible ("7 of 12 favourited") and holds the two actions that matter: clear, and export. Every word and photograph on the page lives in one committed JSON file, src/data/album.json — swap the names, date, venue, credit line, captions, FAQ answers, and the twelve files in static/images/, and the gallery is yours. Design tokens (charcoal surfaces, ivory type, a single muted-gold accent, and both Google Fonts) sit at the top of one stylesheet. Under the hood it is a Gatsby 5 static build with React 18 and TypeScript: typed content models, favourites and CSV logic in small typed utilities, an ESLint flat config, semantic keyboard-accessible controls with visible focus states, reduced-motion support, and layouts verified down to a 320px viewport. There is no server, no accounts, and no environment variables — the build output is a folder of static files.

Podcast apps bury the back catalog and can't link to a moment, so when a listener is told "skip to the bit about tape ninety," they scrub blindly. Every episode gets its own statically generated page with the same player plus a searchable transcript excerpt that highlights every match, announces the match count, and scrolls the first hit into view; transcripts are server-rendered so they stay readable without JavaScript. The design is a bold audio-first identity — near-black base, rich violet, one acid-lime accent, Bricolage Grotesque display type with Schibsted Grotesk body — implemented as design tokens atop one global stylesheet with CSS Modules per component. Built with Next.js (App Router) and TypeScript using output: 'export', it ships a fully static out/ directory where every episode route loads directly on any static host, lints and type-checks clean, supports reduced motion and visible focus states, and stays responsive down to 320px-wide screens.

Cart-based shop templates assume restocks and live inventory, which is exactly wrong for this kind of selling: each piece exists once, releases happen at an announced time, and the fastest email wins. Drop sells that ritual instead — a release the audience can watch approaching, pieces that visibly die when they are claimed, and rules stated plainly enough that nobody argues about who was first.

The masthead is a huge JetBrains Mono countdown ticking to the configured drop datetime, over an acid-orange marquee ticker that repeats the drop facts. Below it, eight pieces hang in a brutalist grid with era, size, condition, and price on every card. Before the drop, available pieces carry a "Drops Fri" chip and an "Ask about this piece" button that opens a pre-filled question email; the moment the datetime passes, the page flips in the browser to a giant LIVE NOW state — chips turn AVAILABLE and buttons become "Claim by email" with a CLAIM subject line, no redeploy needed. Sold pieces are unmistakably gone: greyscale photo, rotated SOLD stamp, struck-through price with a GONE flag, and no action at all. A three-step "How a drop works" section, an honesty strip explaining that SOLD stamps are updated by hand (no cart, no live stock counter), and a five-question FAQ with FAQPage JSON-LD round out the page.

Countdown math, the upcoming/live state machine, date formatting, and the mailto builder are small typed modules in src/utils, and design tokens sit at the top of one CSS file. Technically it is React 19 in React Router framework mode with ssr disabled and the route prerendered, so npm run build emits plain static HTML that any static host can serve, hydrated only to run the clock. Semantic markup, a keyboard-accessible native-details FAQ, visible focus states, reduced-motion fallbacks, and layouts verified down to 320px wide come standard.

templates.name: Changelog
templates.summary: A product release-notes site with instant feature/fix filters and a marker for everything that shipped since a visitor's last look.
templates.description:
Changelog is a static release-notes site for a shipping product — a SaaS, a developer tool, an app — whose team wants its progress to be visible and easy to trust. Release notes scattered across Slack messages, emails, and tweets convince nobody; a changelog that reads like part of the product does. Every entry here is a plain markdown file with four frontmatter fields (title, date, version, tags), so publishing a release note is a commit, not a CMS session.

The index lays all releases on a vertical timeline with a date rail, monospace version chips, and colored tag chips — emerald Feature, amber Fix, indigo Improvement. Filter chips narrow the timeline to features or fixes instantly, with per-tag counts and a live "Showing X of Y releases" line, all without a reload. The signature behavior is the last-visit marker: the browser stores the time of a visitor's last look in localStorage, and on their next visit every newer release gets a New badge and a highlighted timeline node, an indigo "New since your last visit" divider (labeled with that date) separates new from seen, and a hero banner counts the new releases. A first visit shows no marker — the timestamp is saved silently. Each entry also gets a statically prerendered permalink page at /releases/<slug>/ with newer/older navigation cards, code blocks are syntax-highlighted by Shiki, an RSS feed at /rss.xml lists every release, and a four-question FAQ ships with FAQPage JSON-LD. The seed content documents five believable releases of Relaycast, a fictional webhook-delivery platform, spread across three months.

Personalizing is deliberately small: add or edit markdown files in src/content/changelog/ (validated by a zod collection schema) and change the product name, tagline, links, and FAQ copy in src/data/site.json. The visual direction is a crisp modern-SaaS changelog — white and cool zinc neutrals, indigo primary, Hanken Grotesk with Fira Code for versions and code, a dot-grid hero with a decorative delivery-log terminal panel — implemented as design tokens at the top of one hand-written stylesheet. Built on Astro's content collections with TypeScript throughout, the filter and last-visit logic live as small typed utilities driving a vanilla-TypeScript island; the project lints, type-checks, and builds clean, and every route loads directly and stays overflow-free down to a 320px viewport.

The shipped demo demonstrates these capabilities directly. Standout details include Vertical release timeline, Instant feature/fix filter, New-since-your-last-visit marker, Markdown entries with permalink pages, and Markdown entry bodies. Its content and state strategy uses device-local localStorage state. The stack uses Astro (static output, content collections). Presentation uses plain hand-written CSS with design tokens in one stylesheet. This gives evaluators a working, customizable foundation rather than a static visual concept.

No keys are collected, no proxy exists, and a visible note says so. The seeded content documents Hooklane, a fictional webhook delivery API with four endpoints spread across GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE, so the shape of a finished reference is visible before a single edit.

In the try panel, labelled inputs — text fields, numeric fields, and selects for enums and booleans — live-update a syntax-highlighted, terminal-styled curl block: query params become readable -G --data-urlencode lines, path params are URI-encoded into the URL, and body params are typed into pretty-printed JSON. The copy button copies exactly the visible text, the form state syncs into the page URL as you type, and a shared link restores the same filled state — server-side too, so restored examples work before JavaScript loads, and a plain GET form submit covers the no-JS case entirely. Technically it is a NestJS 12 server (ESM, strict TypeScript) rendering Handlebars views with escaping on, an ESLint flat config with typescript-eslint, and an original dark code-editor design system — near-black canvas, elevated panels, a syntax-spectrum hairline, Red Hat Display and Red Hat Mono — with semantic labelled controls, visible focus states, and layouts verified down to 320 px.

Every change updates the preview instantly and regenerates the template snippet under one deterministic rule — required props always appear, optional props appear only when they differ from the component's default, and long tags wrap one attribute per line — so the snippet matches the current configuration exactly. A copy button puts that markup on the clipboard with a confirmation, each playground's last configuration persists per device in localStorage and restores after reload, and "Reset props" returns to the documented start and forgets the saved copy. Technically it is Vue 3 with strict TypeScript and Vite, vue-router with direct-load support on static hosts (the build emits a 404.html SPA fallback plus an honest not-found page), ESLint flat config, vue-tsc type-checking in the build, semantic labelled controls with visible focus states, and layouts verified down to 320 px with no horizontal overflow.

templates.description:
Engineering Blog is a publishing home for a technical team that writes publicly — postmortems, design writeups, and running-in-production notes. Fenced code blocks render at build time onto a dark, crisply contrasting surface with a language label, custom cool-toned syntax highlighting, and a copy button that copies the code exactly (verified byte-for-byte) with a Copied confirmation — added after hydration, so prose stays fully readable without JavaScript. Each post shows a reading time computed in a typed utility from prose word count plus code-line count. Posts sharing a series name are stitched together: a crimson thread connects them in the index list, each post carries a series chip with its part label, and previous/next series navigation links the parts to each other. The index lists every post with date, tags, reading time, and excerpt, followed by an about section with the authors and a four-question FAQ that emits FAQPage JSON-LD; every post adds BlogPosting JSON-LD.

The visual identity is a cool editorial reading experience: pure white and cool zinc surfaces, near-black ink, one crimson accent, Newsreader serif prose at a ~68ch measure with Source Sans 3 UI and Courier Prime code, and an original SVG pennant wordmark — no photography anywhere. Under the hood it is a Gatsby 5 static build with React 18 and TypeScript: gatsby-transformer-remark with Prism highlighting, typed utilities for reading time, series resolution, and dates, an ESLint flat config, semantic article markup with keyboard-accessible controls and visible focus states, and layouts verified down to a 320px viewport with code blocks scrolling internally rather than breaking the page.
